newsitem.title: POLAND: POLAND ALLOWS 400,000 T DUTY-FREE DIESEL IMPORTS.
newsitem.headline: POLAND ALLOWS 400,000 T DUTY-FREE DIESEL IMPORTS.

text.p: Poland has decided to allow duty-free import of 400,000 tonnes of diesel fuel until December 15, the Government Information Office said in a statement on Thursday.

It said the finance minister had also introduced temporary limits on retail price rises for domestically-produced engine fuels, saying the maximum increase for Polish diesel was 4.9 percent above prices applying before the government decision was made on Tuesday.

To compensate producers and importers for rises in the price of crude oil and engine fuels on international markets, the minister, Grzegorz Kolodko, had also ordered a partial suspension of excise tax on domestic and imported diesel fuel.

"In order to improve the profitability of production and import of diesel oil, and to limit the growth in retail prices, the cabinet decided to introduce a duty-free contingent amounting to 400,000 tonnes to be realised by December 15," the statement, reported by PAP news agency, said.
It gave no details of the proposed reduction in excise tax.

Last week industry officials said Polish diesel prices had risen 15 to 25 percent over recent weeks as retailers sold fuel bought from state reserves during weekly auctions at above official price ceilings set for domestically-produced fuels.
The government last month unlocked state reserves of diesel to avoid market shortages at a time of high demand, especially from farmers, coinciding with a steep rise in world oil prices.
At an auction on October 2, when the industry ministry offered 100,000 tonnes of fuel, prices ranged between 1.19 and 1.41 zlotys per litre.
Poland's biggest distributor, CPN, said earlier on Thursday that Poland was about to face shortages of the popular cheap 94-octane leaded petrol.

"I estimate between 30 and 40 percent of our stations will have this kind of petrol, while the rest will have only other kinds," said Stefan Olczyk, sales director of state-owned CPN which controls nearly 1,400 of Poland's 4,700 stations.
High world oil prices coupled with domestic caps on prices of Polish-made liquid fuels have made it unattractive for domestic refiners to produce them.

Olczyk said the shortage would arise because the large Plock refinery had curbed sales and it was not profitable to import the 94-octane leaded petrol, which remains popular because of the large number of old cars running on this fuel.

He added that diesel, which had been unavailable in some regions over the last few weeks, was now in steady supply after CPN's additional purchases from state reserves and following imports, but its price was higher in some regions. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
